opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core value comes down to this: a lot of the decisions we care about most, like policy changes, the design of a new social platform, or how an organization is structured, play out over long horizons and through the interactions of many people. Those are exactly the decisions that are hardest to test in the real world. You can't really A/B test a tax policy across a whole society for ten years, and by the time you see the consequences, it's often too late to undo them.

Simulation gives us a kind of sandbox where we can ask "what if" questions before committing. That idea isn't new. Social scientists and economists have used agent-based models for decades. The limitation has always been that the agents were quite simple: a few hand-written rules, maybe a utility function. They could capture some aggregate dynamics, but they couldn't capture the richness of how real people reason, remember, form relationships, and change their minds over time. That richness is often what drives the long-term outcomes we actually care about.

What's exciting now, and what motivated our work on generative agents, is that large language models let us build agents that behave in much more believable, human-like ways. They can remember past experiences, reflect on them, make plans, and respond to one another. When you put many of these agents together, you start to see emergent social behavior, like information spreading through a community or people coordinating around an event, that nobody explicitly scripted.

So the value isn't that simulation gives you a crystal ball. It doesn't, and I think it's important to be humble about that. The value is that it lets you explore the space of plausible futures, surface second- and third-order effects you might not have anticipated, and stress-test your intuitions. If you're designing a community or a policy, you can see how things might unfold over weeks or months of simulated time, notice failure modes early, and iterate.

Longer term, I see these simulations as a tool for better collective decision-making: a way to rehearse the future before we have to live it. That comes with real responsibility. We need to validate these models carefully against real human behavior and be clear about where they're reliable and where they aren't.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulating many agents interacting over weeks or months to explore emergent behavior and second- and third-order effects, extending beyond isolated questions asked one at a time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core value is that simulation lets you ask "what if" in a space where the stakes of being wrong are basically zero, and where the feedback loop is fast enough that you can actually learn something.

When you make a decision in the real world, a policy, a product change, a shift in how a community is governed, the consequences unfold over months or years, and you only ever get to run that experiment once. You can't rewind. You can't try the counterfactual. So most of our understanding of long-term effects is retrospective and, frankly, anecdotal. We tell stories after the fact about why something worked or didn't.

What simulation offers is a kind of prototyping for social and institutional decisions, the same way an architect builds a model before pouring concrete. With generative agents in particular, the thing that excites me is that the agents aren't just following scripted rules. They have something like memory, they reflect, they form plans, they react to each other. So when you introduce a change into that world, you get emergent behavior that you didn't hand-author. Sometimes it surprises you, and that surprise is exactly the signal you want, because it points at a second-order effect you hadn't considered.

Now, I want to be careful here. A simulation is not a prediction. The agents are built on language models trained on human-generated data, so they reflect patterns in how people tend to behave, but they aren't the specific people who will live with your decision. I think of the output less as "this is what will happen" and more as "here is a plausible space of things that could happen, and here are the dynamics that drive them." It widens your imagination about consequences. It helps you notice the failure modes early, when they're cheap to address.

And there's a second benefit that I think gets underrated, which is that it changes the conversation among the people making the decision. When you can show stakeholders a living, observable world where their proposal plays out, the discussion stops being purely about abstract arguments and starts being about concrete scenarios. You can point at something and say, "Look, this is where it breaks down." That tends to produce better deliberation, even if the simulation itself is imperfect.

So I'd summarize it this way: simulation won't tell you the future, but it gives you a rehearsal space for it. And for decisions whose effects are slow, irreversible, and tangled up in human behavior, having any rehearsal at all is a big step up from having none.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents reacting to each other, producing emergent behavior and second-order effects, and frames simulation as a rehearsal space that widens the range of plausible consequences. This communicates exploration beyond isolated questions asked one at a time.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is that simulation gives us a way to ask “what if?” before we make a decision in the real world. A decision might look reasonable when you consider its immediate effects, but once people respond to it—and respond to one another—you can get consequences that are much harder to anticipate.

I wouldn’t treat a simulation as a prediction of exactly what will happen. It’s a way to explore possible outcomes and make our assumptions explicit. What are we assuming about how people behave? Does the outcome change if those assumptions change? Who might benefit, and who might experience a cost that we hadn’t considered?

That can help us make better decisions, but it can also help us ask better questions. Sometimes the most useful thing a simulation reveals is what we still need to learn from people before moving forward.

r001.rationale: The response describes exploring how people respond to a decision and to one another, testing changing assumptions, and considering multiple outcomes—framing simulation as more than isolated questions asked one at a time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is that simulation gives us a way to explore possible futures before we commit to a decision. A lot of decisions have consequences that emerge over time, through interactions between people, and those consequences can be difficult to anticipate by looking at each person or each decision in isolation.

If we can build a simulation that captures some of those dynamics, we can ask, “What might happen if we introduce this policy? What changes if we make a different choice?” And we can look for unintended consequences or outcomes that we hadn’t considered.

But I would frame that as exploration, rather than prediction. A simulation is built on assumptions, and it can be wrong. Its value is in helping us identify those assumptions, ask better questions, and decide what we need to investigate in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response explains that long-term effects emerge through interactions over time and are hard to anticipate by examining each person or decision in isolation, framing simulation as a way to explore those broader dynamics.
